title: The occasion: Ralegh's last verses
short: Traditionally written the night before Ralegh's execution (29 October 1618) and found in his Bible in the Gatehouse.
body: Sir Walter Ralegh was beheaded at Westminster on 29 October 1618, after the failure of his last voyage to Guiana revived a death sentence passed in 1603. Early copies say these lines were written in his Bible the night before, in the Gatehouse prison at Westminster. Editors of Ralegh's poems (Latham, Rudick) record that the first six lines adapt the last stanza of an earlier Ralegh poem ('Nature, that washed her hands in milk', titled in one copy as on his mistress Serena), with the final couplet added. The poem is thus a love poem's conclusion turned into an epitaph. The archive's title 'The Conclusion' is one of several in early copies.

title: takes in trust
short: Time is a dishonest trustee or banker, who receives our goods for safekeeping and repays them only with dust.
body: To 'take in trust' is to receive property to hold for another. The metaphor is financial and legal: Time takes charge of youth, joys and everything we have, and 'pays us but with earth and dust'. Ralegh, who had lived through spectacular wealth and ruin, makes Time a defaulting steward. The word 'trust' returns at the end of the poem in a new, religious sense, faith in God.

title: earth and dust
short: From Genesis 3:19 and the burial service: 'earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust'.
body: The payment Time makes is the grave. The phrase echoes God's sentence on Adam, 'dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return' (Genesis 3:19), and the committal in the Book of Common Prayer burial service, 'earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust; in sure and certain hope of the resurrection'. That hope of resurrection is what the final couplet supplies.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Genesis 3:19

title: Shuts up the story of our days
short: Time closes the book of our lives, as one shuts a finished story; the grave is the last page.
body: When we have 'wander'd all our ways', travelled every road of life, Time 'shuts up' our story, closes it like a book. The image suits a man who had written The History of the World (1614) in the Tower and wrote these lines in a Bible. 'Shut up' also means to imprison or confine, which recalls Ralegh's long imprisonments. The finality of 'shuts up' is the low point of the poem before the turn of the couplet.

title: My God shall raise me up, I trust
short: The added couplet turns despair to faith in resurrection, echoing Job 19:25-26 and repeating 'trust' in a new sense.
body: The final couplet, added to the borrowed stanza, overturns it. The repeated 'this earth, this grave, this dust' points to the very things Time paid us with, and turns them into the place of resurrection. The language recalls Job 19:25-26 ('though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God'), read in the burial service. 'I trust' reverses the corrupt 'trust' of line 1: Time betrays trust, God keeps it. Some early copies read 'The Lord will raise me up'.

anchor: this earth, this grave, this dust
title: Form
short: Eight iambic tetrameter lines: an alternately rhymed quatrain, a couplet, and the added closing couplet.
body: The rhyme scheme is abab cc dd. The first six lines are the inherited stanza, which in the original poem ended with the couplet 'ways/days'. Ralegh's addition repeats the 'dust/trust' rhyme from lines 1 and 3, so that the new couplet answers the opening rhymes directly. The tetrameter gives the poem the plainness of an epitaph. The triple repetition 'this earth, this grave, this dust' gathers the nouns of the first stanza and points to them, as if the speaker were standing at his own grave.

anchor: Our youth, our joys, our all
title: Our youth, our joys, our all
short: A climactic list: Time takes youth, then pleasures, then everything we own.
body: The line builds by stages to 'our all we have', a phrase that turns the list into a total. The first-person plural makes the poem general, an epitaph for everyone, until the 'My God' and 'me' of the final couplet make it personal. The financial metaphor of trust continues: these are the goods deposited with Time, and the next lines describe how they are repaid. The language of totality, 'our all', makes the loss seem complete before the couplet reverses it.

title: the dark and silent grave
short: The grave is where Time pays us out and closes our story: dark, silent, final.
body: The relative clause 'Who in the dark and silent grave ... Shuts up the story' makes Time itself the agent who locks us in the grave. Darkness and silence are the absence of the senses and of speech, the opposite of story and song. The phrase prepares the reversal of the final couplet, in which the same grave becomes the place from which God will raise the speaker.

title: wander’d all our ways
short: Life as a journey or pilgrimage, with a suggestion of straying; Ralegh had literally travelled far.
body: To have 'wander'd all our ways' is to have finished our life's journeys, with a hint of erring or straying. Ralegh, explorer of Virginia and Guiana, had travelled further than most, and the line gains force from the circumstances. The biblical sense of human life as wandering (as in Hebrews 11:13, where the faithful confess 'that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth') lies behind it.

sources.cite: Bible (KJV), Hebrews 11:13
